Literal Sense

The Setting: Isaac's Old Age and Blindness

Genesis 27 opens with Isaac in his old age, his eyes dimmed by years: "And it came to pass that Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim, and he could not see" (Gen 27:1). The patriarch, believing his death to be near, summons his elder son Esau to receive the paternal blessing. This blessing was no mere formality but carried prophetic weight and covenantal significance, transferring the patriarchal authority and the promises made to Abraham.

Isaac's request to Esau is specific: "Take thy arms, thy quiver, and bow, and go abroad: and when thou hast taken some thing by hunting, make me savoury meat thereof, as thou knowest I like, and bring it, that I may eat: and my soul may bless thee before I die" (Gen 27:3-4). The connection between the meal and the blessing reflects ancient Near Eastern custom, where significant covenantal acts were often accompanied by ceremonial meals.

Rebekah's Plan

Rebekah overhears Isaac's instructions to Esau and immediately sets her own plan in motion. She tells Jacob: "Go thy way to the flock, bring me two kids of the best, that I may make of them meat for thy father, such as he gladly eateth: Which when thou hast brought in, and he hath eaten, he may bless thee before he die" (Gen 27:9-10).

The question of Rebekah's motivation has occupied commentators throughout the centuries. She had received a divine oracle before the twins' birth: "Two nations are in thy womb, and two peoples shall be divided out of thy womb, and one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger" (Gen 25:23). Theodoret of Cyrus, in his Questions on Genesis, suggests that "the sequel showed that she was directed by God in this delicate business."

Theodoret of Cyrus, Questions on Genesis, 78

Jacob's Hesitation

Jacob's initial objection reveals not moral compunction but fear of detection: "Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am smooth: If my father shall feel me, and perceive it, I fear lest he think I would have mocked him, and I bring upon me a curse instead of a blessing" (Gen 27:11-12). Jacob is concerned about the practical consequences of failure rather than the ethical dimension of deception.

Rebekah answers decisively: "Upon me be thy curse, my son: only hear my voice, and go, fetch me them" (Gen 27:13). She takes full responsibility for the plan, willing to bear any consequences that might follow.

The Disguise

Rebekah prepares both the meal and the disguise with care: "And she put on him very good garments of Esau, which she had at home with her: And the little skins of the kids she put about his hands, and covered the bare of his neck" (Gen 27:15-16). Esau's garments would carry his distinctive scent, while the goatskins would mimic the hairiness of Esau's arms and neck. The deception engages multiple senses: taste (the savory meat), touch (the hairy hands), smell (Esau's garments), and sound (Jacob's voice, which proves problematic).

The Dialogue with Isaac

The encounter between Jacob and Isaac is filled with dramatic tension. Jacob approaches and announces himself falsely: "I am Esau thy firstborn: I have done as thou badest me: arise, sit, and eat of my venison, that thy soul may bless me" (Gen 27:19). When Isaac expresses surprise at the speed of the hunt, Jacob compounds his deception with blasphemy: "It was the will of God that what I sought came quickly in my way" (Gen 27:20).

Isaac remains suspicious: "The voice indeed is the voice of Jacob: but the hands are the hands of Esau" (Gen 27:22). Yet after feeling Jacob's hands and smelling Esau's garments, the patriarch proceeds to bless his son. St. John Chrysostom, in Homily 53 on Genesis, explains that God permitted Isaac to be "in darkness respecting this affair, that it might be more manifest that the will of man had no part in preferring Jacob."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis, 53

The Blessing of Jacob

Isaac's blessing is comprehensive and prophetic: "God give thee of the dew of heaven, and of the fatness of the earth, abundance of corn and wine. And let peoples serve thee, and tribes worship thee: be thou lord of thy brethren, and let thy mother's children bow down before thee. Cursed be he that curseth thee: and let him that blesseth thee be filled with blessings" (Gen 27:28-29). The blessing echoes the Abrahamic covenant, promising material prosperity, dominion over peoples, and the protective divine presence.

Esau's Return and Isaac's Trembling

The dramatic reversal occurs when Esau returns from his hunt: "He also had made ready savory meats, and brought them in to his father, saying: Arise, my father, and eat of thy son's venison; that thy soul may bless me" (Gen 27:31). Isaac's response is visceral: "Isaac was struck with fear, and astonished exceedingly" (Gen 27:33). The Hebrew text describes a "great trembling" that seized the patriarch.

According to the Haydock Commentary citing St. Augustine's Questions on Genesis (Question 80), the Septuagint translates this moment as Isaac being "rapt into an ecstasy exceedingly great," during which God revealed to him the meaning of what had transpired, so that he would not think of revoking the blessing.

St. Augustine, Questions on Genesis, 80

Esau's Bitter Cry

Esau's response is one of the most poignant moments in Genesis: "Esau hearing his father's words, roared out with a great cry: and being in a consternation, said: Bless me also, my father... Hast thou not reserved me also a blessing?" (Gen 27:34, 36). The Hebrew verb for Esau's cry (tza'akah) denotes an anguished scream. Isaac confirms that the blessing given to Jacob cannot be withdrawn: "I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed" (Gen 27:33).

Isaac does grant Esau a secondary blessing, though it is more of a prophecy of hardship: "In the fatness of the earth, and in the dew of heaven from above, shall thy blessing be. Thou shalt live by the sword, and shalt serve thy brother: and the time shall come, when thou shalt shake off and loose his yoke from thy neck" (Gen 27:39-40). The blessing is inverted: while Jacob receives the dew from above, Esau's portion places the fatness of earth first, and his fate includes servitude and warfare.

Esau's Hatred and Jacob's Flight

The chapter concludes with Esau's murderous intent: "Esau therefore always hated Jacob, for the blessing wherewith his father had blessed him: and he said in his heart: The days will come of the mourning of my father, and I will kill my brother Jacob" (Gen 27:41). Rebekah, learning of this threat, arranges for Jacob to flee to her brother Laban in Haran, framing the journey to Isaac as a mission to find a proper wife from among their kindred rather than from the Canaanites.

Allegorical Sense

Jacob and Esau as Types of Church and Synagogue

The Church Fathers consistently interpreted Jacob and Esau as types representing two peoples: the Church (the younger) and the Synagogue (the elder). St. Augustine develops this typology extensively in City of God, Book XVI, Chapter 37:

"Isaac's two sons, Esau and Jacob, grew up together. The primacy of the elder was transferred to the younger by a bargain and agreement between them... Isaac is the law and the prophecy: even by the mouth of the Jews Christ is blessed by prophecy as by one who knows not, because it is itself not understood."

St. Augustine, City of God, XVI.37

Augustine further explains the prophetic significance of Isaac's blessing: "The blessing of Jacob is therefore a proclamation of Christ to all nations. It is this which has come to pass, and is now being fulfilled." The patriarch's words about the dew of heaven, the abundance of corn and wine, and the service of nations find their fulfillment not in earthly Israel but in the Church of Christ, which has spread to every nation.

St. Augustine, City of God, XVI.37

The Mystery of the Deception

The moral difficulty of Jacob's deception troubled many readers, but the Fathers resolved this by reading the narrative as prophetic mystery rather than mere historical deception. St. Augustine addresses this directly in Contra Mendacium (Against Lying), Chapter 10:

"If it be no lie, when things which signify one thing by another are referred to the understanding of a truth, assuredly not only that which Jacob did or said to his father that he might be blessed" should not be considered lying, but rather as a figure or "mystery" pointing to the preference which was afterwards to be given to the Gentiles before the carnal Jews.

St. Augustine, Contra Mendacium, 10

The Haydock Commentary, drawing on Augustine, explains that Jacob "may be excused from a lie, because this whole passage was mysterious, as relating to the preference which was afterwards to be given to the Gentiles before the carnal Jews, which Jacob by prophetic light might understand."

Haydock Commentary on Genesis 27

Irenaeus on Jacob as Type of Christ

St. Irenaeus of Lyons, in Against Heresies, Book IV, Chapter 21, presents Jacob as a type of Christ in his supplanting of the elder brother:

"At his birth, since he laid hold on his brother's heel, he was called Jacob, that is, the supplanter one who holds, but is not held; binding the feet, but not being bound; striving and conquering; grasping in his hand his adversary's heel, that is, victory. For to this end was the Lord born, the type of whose birth he set forth beforehand."

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, IV.21

Irenaeus continues: "Jacob received the rights of the first-born, when his brother looked on them with contempt; even as also the younger nation received Him, Christ, the first-begotten, when the elder nation rejected Him... In Christ every blessing is summed up, and therefore the latter people has snatched away the blessings of the former from the Father, just as Jacob took away the blessing of this Esau."

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, IV.21

Rebekah as Type of the Blessed Virgin Mary

In Catholic Marian tradition, particularly as developed by St. Louis de Montfort in True Devotion to Mary, Rebekah serves as a type of the Blessed Virgin. Just as Rebekah prepared Jacob to receive the blessing of Isaac, so Mary prepares sinners to receive the blessing of the heavenly Father:

"Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort sees Rebekah as a type of Mary, preparing sinners (Jacob) to obtain the Father's (Isaac's) blessing."

St. Louis de Montfort, True Devotion to Mary, 183-200

In this allegory, Isaac symbolizes the Heavenly Father, Esau symbolizes the firstborn (representing those who rely on their own merits), Jacob symbolizes the elect who receive grace through Mary's intercession, and Rebekah prefigures the Blessed Virgin who clothes her children in the merits of Christ. As Rebekah clothed Jacob in Esau's garments, so Mary clothes believers in the righteousness of Christ, her firstborn Son.

The Goatskins and Christ's Righteousness

The goatskins that covered Jacob's hands and neck have been interpreted as a type of how believers are clothed in Christ's righteousness. Just as Jacob appeared before Isaac covered in another's garments to receive the blessing, so Christians appear before God the Father clothed in Christ's righteousness to receive eternal blessing:

"Jacob realizes that he does not have to earn Isaac's favor himself. If he can appear to be Esau when he goes to Isaac, and if Isaac thinks that he is, in fact, Esau, Jacob will receive the father's blessing as if he was really Esau."

Traditional typological interpretation

The covering of animal skins also recalls Genesis 3:21, where God clothed Adam and Eve with "garments of skins" after their sin. This covering, provided only through sacrifice, prefigures Christ's righteousness covering sinful humanity. As Carmelite tradition notes, some have compared the goatskins on Jacob's hands and neck to the Brown Scapular, a sign of Mary's protection and Christ's covering.

Isaac's Blindness and the Blindness of Israel

Isaac's physical blindness, which allowed Jacob to receive the blessing, has been read allegorically as representing Israel's spiritual blindness regarding the Messiah. St. John Chrysostom observes that God permitted Isaac to remain "in darkness respecting this affair" so that divine providence rather than human will would be manifest in Jacob's election.

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis, 53

St. Augustine in his Sermon 72 on the New Testament develops this theme further: "The name of Abraham was to be developed in this world; for here he was made the father of many nations, whence he received his name. But the name of Israel relates to another world, where we shall see God. Therefore the people of God, the Christian people in this present time, is both Jacob and Israel, Jacob in fact, Israel in hope."

St. Augustine, Sermon 72 on the New Testament

The Blessing of Corn and Wine

Isaac's blessing includes "abundance of corn and wine" (Gen 27:28), which Augustine interprets eucharistically: "The world like a field is filled with the odor of Christ's name: His is the blessing of the dew of heaven, that is, of the showers of divine words; and of the fruitfulness of the earth, that is, of the gathering together of the peoples: His is the plenty of corn and wine, that is, the multitude that gathers bread and wine in the sacrament of His body and blood."

St. Augustine, City of God, XVI.37

The Transfer of the Birthright

The transfer of blessing from the elder to the younger son echoes throughout Scripture: Abel over Cain, Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Ephraim over Manasseh, David the youngest over his brothers. Irenaeus sees in this pattern a consistent divine pedagogy: "The children brought forth by Rebecca were a prediction of the two nations; and that the one should be indeed the greater, but the other the less; that the one also should be under bondage, but the other free; but both should be of one and the same Father."

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, IV.21

This pattern finds its fulfillment in the New Covenant, where the Gentiles (the younger people) receive the blessing while many in Israel (the elder people) reject it. As Augustine notes: "The younger people is called the Supplanter of its brother the elder people... Have we supplanted the Jews? No, but we are said to be their supplanters, for that for our sakes they were supplanted."

St. Augustine, Sermon 72 on the New Testament
moral:
Moral Sense

The Danger of Despising Spiritual Blessings

Esau's tragedy begins not in Genesis 27 but in Genesis 25, when he sold his birthright for a bowl of lentils. The Epistle to the Hebrews warns: "Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau; who for one mess, sold his first birthright. For know ye that afterwards, when he desired to inherit the benediction, he was rejected; for he found no place of repentance, although with tears he had sought it" (Heb 12:16-17).

The moral lesson is stark: Esau despised what was sacred for what was temporal. He valued immediate gratification over lasting blessing. As one commentary observes: "Esau takes the promises of God so lightly and considers them of such little value that he is willing to trade them for a single meal." This serves as a warning to all who would trade eternal goods for temporal pleasures.

The Consequences of Parental Favoritism

The narrative reveals the destructive effects of Isaac's favoritism toward Esau and Rebekah's favoritism toward Jacob: "Isaac loved Esau, because he ate of his hunting: and Rebecca loved Jacob" (Gen 25:28). This divided house produces deception, conflict, and ultimately the separation of the family. Parents are warned against showing preference among their children, which breeds resentment and rivalry.

Isaac's intention to bless Esau despite the divine oracle to Rebekah also raises questions about his own spiritual discernment. Was he acting in faith or in partiality? Chrysostom suggests that God allowed Isaac's blindness precisely to demonstrate that the blessing was according to divine will, not human preference.

The Complexity of Human Motives

The moral texture of Genesis 27 resists simple categorization. Rebekah acts to fulfill a divine oracle, but she employs deception. Jacob obeys his mother, but he lies to his father. Isaac intends to bless his son, but he ignores God's revealed will. Esau grieves his loss, but he had earlier despised the birthright.

Theodoret of Cyrus notes that the outcome suggests divine involvement: "The sequel showed that she was directed by God in this delicate business." Yet this does not mean God approved of the means employed. Rather, as Irenaeus observed, God's foreknowledge does not negate human free will but works through the complex web of human choices to accomplish His purposes.

Theodoret of Cyrus, Questions on Genesis, 78

Jacob's Fear Rather Than Conscience

Jacob's hesitation before the deception reveals a troubling moral state. He objects not because the plan is wrong but because he fears getting caught: "I fear lest he think I would have mocked him, and I bring upon me a curse instead of a blessing" (Gen 27:12). As commentators note: "Many point out that Jacob is not protesting his mother's plan out of moral compunction, but out of the fear of being caught. Jacob is willing to go along with the plan, but he wants to make sure he is protected first."

The moral warning is clear: fear of consequences is not the same as conviction of sin. True moral formation requires not merely prudent calculation but genuine love of what is good and hatred of what is evil. Jacob's character requires decades of divine discipline before he becomes Israel, the one who "wrestled with God and prevailed."

The Sin of Lying

Jacob's statements to Isaac are direct lies: "I am Esau thy firstborn" (Gen 27:19) and "It was the will of God that what I sought came quickly in my way" (Gen 27:20). The second statement compounds the deception with blasphemy, invoking God's name to support a falsehood.

While the Fathers recognized the typological significance of the narrative, they did not thereby excuse lying in ordinary circumstances. Augustine's treatment in Contra Mendacium carefully distinguishes between prophetic figures and ordinary moral obligations. The mystical significance of the event does not establish deception as morally permissible for those who lack prophetic authorization.

The Consequences of Sin

Jacob's deception, though it obtains the blessing, also initiates a cascade of consequences. He must flee from Esau's murderous anger. He will not see his mother again she dies before his return. He himself will be deceived by Laban regarding his brides. He will watch his own sons deceive him regarding Joseph. The deceiver becomes the deceived: "Jacob himself is deceived later on (29:1-30), which is probably talionic ('eye for an eye') retribution for his own lies."

The moral principle is that sin carries consequences even when forgiven. Jacob receives the blessing and becomes the heir of the promise, but he also reaps what he has sown. Divine mercy does not eliminate the natural consequences of our choices.

Esau's Bitter Repentance

Esau's grief is genuine and moving: "Esau hearing his father's words, roared out with a great cry" (Gen 27:34). Yet Hebrews describes this as a repentance that came too late or was of the wrong kind: "He found no place of repentance, although with tears he had sought it" (Heb 12:17).

The Fathers distinguish between true repentance (metanoia), which involves a change of heart and life, and mere regret for lost benefits. Esau weeps for what he has lost, not necessarily for what he has done wrong. He had not valued the blessing when it was his to keep; now he grieves because another has taken it. True repentance requires not just sorrow for consequences but genuine contrition for sin and amendment of life.

Divine Providence and Human Responsibility

The patristic interpretation maintains both divine sovereignty and human responsibility. Ambrosiaster writes: "There is no respect of persons in God's foreknowledge. For God's foreknowledge is that by which it is defined what the future will of each person will be, in which he will either be condemned or rewarded... God will call whomever he knows will obey, and he will not call whomever he knows will not obey."

Ambrosiaster, Commentary on Romans

Irenaeus affirms that God's foreknowledge "does not preclude any notion of election that negates free-will. For Irenaeus, the reason why God loved Jacob and hated Esau was because God is the one 'who knows all things before they can come to pass'" presumably, He foreknows how each person will freely choose to respond to grace.

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies

The Call to Examine Our Own Hearts

The moral complexity of Genesis 27 invites readers to examine their own hearts. Do we, like Esau, despise spiritual blessings for temporal satisfactions? Do we, like Jacob, pursue good ends through questionable means? Do we, like Isaac, allow our preferences to cloud our discernment of God's will? Do we, like Rebekah, take matters into our own hands rather than trusting God's timing?

St. John Chrysostom encourages believers to learn from both the virtues and the faults of the patriarchs, recognizing that God works through flawed human beings to accomplish His saving purposes.
anagogical:
Anagogical Sense

The Blessing and the Heavenly Inheritance

The anagogical sense of Genesis 27 directs our vision toward the eternal inheritance that awaits the children of God. Isaac's blessing of Jacob with "the dew of heaven, and of the fatness of the earth" (Gen 27:28) points beyond temporal prosperity to the heavenly blessings reserved for the elect. The blessing that could not be revoked foreshadows the irrevocable nature of God's gifts and calling: "For the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance" (Rom 11:29).

St. Irenaeus, in Against Heresies Book V, Chapter 33, interprets Isaac's blessing eschatologically: "The blessing of Isaac with which he blessed his younger son Jacob has the same meaning, when he says, Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed." Irenaeus continues: "But the field is the world," understanding the blessing as referring to the eschatological kingdom.

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, V.33

The Two Peoples and the Final Judgment

Jacob and Esau, representing the Church and those outside the covenant, point toward the final separation of humanity. As Augustine observes in City of God: "Esau and Jacob represent a figure of two peoples, the Jews and the Christians. Jesus Christ descends from the tribe of Judah, Jacob's fourth son." This typology extends to the eschaton, when all humanity will be divided into those who inherit the blessing and those who do not.

St. Augustine, City of God, XVI.37

The irrevocability of Isaac's blessing "I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed" (Gen 27:33) prefigures the finality of the Last Judgment. Once the blessing is given, it cannot be transferred. Once judgment is rendered, it is eternal. Esau's bitter cry and futile tears serve as a warning of the weeping and gnashing of teeth that awaits those who, having despised their inheritance, find themselves excluded from the kingdom.

The Heavenly Garments

The garments of Esau with which Rebekah clothed Jacob point to the heavenly garments promised to the faithful. In Revelation, the saints are clothed in white robes: "They shall walk with me in white, because they are worthy" (Rev 3:4). Just as Jacob could not approach Isaac and receive the blessing in his own garments but needed to be clothed in another's, so believers cannot approach the heavenly Father in their own righteousness but must be clothed in Christ.

The eschatological dimension of this clothing is made explicit in Scripture: "For as many of you as have been baptized in Christ, have put on Christ" (Gal 3:27). This putting on of Christ, begun in baptism, will be completed in the resurrection when "this mortal must put on immortality" (1 Cor 15:53).

Jacob's Name Change and Glorification

Augustine notes in Sermon 72 that "the name of Israel relates to another world, where we shall see God." The name Israel means "one who sees God" or "one who wrestles with God and prevails." Jacob's journey, which begins with the deception in Genesis 27 and culminates in his transformation into Israel at Peniel (Genesis 32), prefigures the believer's journey from this life to the beatific vision.

St. Augustine, Sermon 72 on the New Testament

Augustine further explains: "Therefore the people of God, the Christian people in this present time, is both Jacob and Israel, Jacob in fact, Israel in hope." We are Jacob now pilgrims and supplanters in a foreign land. We shall be Israel in heaven, those who see God face to face.

The Multiplication of the Seed

Isaac's blessing promises that Jacob's descendants will be served by peoples and tribes. This prophecy finds its ultimate fulfillment not in earthly political dominion but in the heavenly assembly described in Revelation: "After this I saw a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne, and in sight of the Lamb" (Rev 7:9). The blessing given to one man extends to an innumerable multitude from every nation.

The Heavenly Jerusalem

The anagogical interpretation of Scripture consistently points earthly realities toward their heavenly counterparts. As the Quadriga method of interpretation explains, a reference to Jerusalem could be understood literally (the physical city), allegorically (the Church), and anagogically (the heavenly Jerusalem). Similarly, the blessing given to Jacob in the house of Isaac points ultimately to the blessing received by the saints in the house of the Father.

John Cassian in the 5th century described anagogical interpretation as "rising from spiritual mysteries even to still more sublime and sacred secrets of heaven." The blessings of corn and wine given to Jacob are transfigured in the heavenly banquet where believers feast with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of God.

Esau's Prophecy and the End Times

Isaac's words to Esau contain an eschatological dimension: "The time shall come, when thou shalt shake off and loose his yoke from thy neck" (Gen 27:40). This prophecy has been understood historically as referring to Edom's rebellion against Israel, but anagogically it points to the final rebellion of the nations against the people of God before the end. Irenaeus notes that such prophecies "must be understood as referring to the appointed kingdom" and warns that those who do not accept this eschatological reading "must fall into much contradiction and contrariety."

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, V.33

The Communion of Saints

The patriarchal blessing, passed from Abraham to Isaac to Jacob, establishes a chain of blessing that extends through all generations to the present day. Believers are incorporated into this chain through faith in Christ, becoming children of Abraham and heirs of the promise. This communion of saints, begun on earth, reaches its perfection in heaven where "many shall come from the east and the west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven" (Matt 8:11).

The Final Rest

Isaac, lying on his bed at the end of his life, blessing his sons before his death, presents an image of the soul at rest in God. The anagogical sense points to the eternal rest promised to the faithful: "There remaineth therefore a day of rest for the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, the same also hath rested from his works, as God did from his" (Heb 4:9-10). Isaac's blessing, given in his last days, prefigures the blessing that the Father will bestow on His children when they enter their eternal rest.

The Final Reconciliation

Though Genesis 27 ends with enmity between the brothers, the later reconciliation of Jacob and Esau (Genesis 33) provides a glimpse of the eschatological peace when "the wolf shall dwell with the lamb" (Isa 11:6). The anagogical sense perceives in human history, with all its conflicts and sorrows, the movement toward that final peace when God shall be all in all, when every tear shall be wiped away, and when the blessing once contested shall be shared by all the redeemed in the kingdom of the Father.
